"Focus" as a noun means a central point — either a precise point in physical space where things converge, or a point in the mind where attention gathers. Every meaning of this word, no matter how different the context, grows from this one core idea: a single, definite spot that everything else is directed toward or organized around.
Meaning 1: The State of Concentrated Attention

The most common everyday meaning. Focus is the mental state in which your attention is fully directed at one thing, free from distraction. Your mind isn't wandering — it is gathered and fixed on a single point, like a spotlight shining brightly on one spot instead of dimly lighting an entire room.

"She studied for hours with complete focus."
"He lost his focus halfway through the lecture."
"After the break, she regained her focus."

When you have focus, you think clearly and work effectively. When you lose it, your attention scatters. Notice that in this meaning, you are the one doing the focusing — focus is something you possess, lose, or regain.
Meaning 2: The Subject or Target of Attention

Focus also names the particular person, thing, or topic that attention is directed at — the thing being focused on, rather than the act of focusing.

"The main focus of today's lesson is grammar."
"Climate change became the focus of the entire conference."
"After the scandal, she became the focus of media attention."

Here, focus is not the mental act — it's the target. Something is the focus. This meaning is very close to saying "the central subject," "the main topic," or "the thing everyone is paying attention to."
Meaning 3: Clarity and Sharpness in Optics and Photography

In the physical world of light and lenses — cameras, telescopes, microscopes, eyeglasses — focus has a precise meaning: the point where light rays meet after passing through a lens or reflecting off a mirror.

When a lens is positioned correctly, light rays from an object converge at exactly one point, and the image looks sharp and clear. When the lens is off, the rays don't meet properly, and the image looks blurry.

"The photograph is in focus." — It is sharp and clear.
"The photograph is out of focus." — It is blurry.
"Adjust the focus of the microscope until the cells are visible."

The focus here is literally a point in space — the precise spot where the light converges. The verb "adjust the focus" means you are moving the lens to shift that convergence point until the image becomes clear.

This meaning also appears metaphorically in everyday speech:

"Her goals are finally coming into focus." (= becoming clearer, more defined)
"The real problem came into focus only after weeks of investigation."
Meaning 4: The Origin Point of an Earthquake (Seismology)

In earthquake science, the focus (also called the hypocenter) is the exact point deep underground where an earthquake originates — where the rock first breaks and releases energy. From this point, seismic waves radiate outward in all directions.

"The earthquake's focus was 20 kilometres below the surface."

The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus is called the epicenter — which is why news reports give the epicenter's location (it's on the surface and can be mapped), while scientists measure the depth of the focus beneath it.
Meaning 5: A Special Defining Point in Geometry

In mathematics, a focus (plural: foci) is a specific fixed point used to define a curve precisely.

  • An ellipse (an oval shape) is defined by two foci. Every single point on the ellipse has a special property: if you measure its distance to one focus and add its distance to the other focus, you always get the same total, no matter where on the ellipse you are.
  • A parabola has one focus. Every point on the parabola is exactly as far from the focus as it is from a fixed line called the directrix.
  • A hyperbola also has two foci, with a similar defining property.

"Mark the two foci of the ellipse on your diagram."

Satellite dishes and car headlights are shaped as parabolas because of the special property of the focus: any signal arriving parallel to the dish's axis reflects directly to the focus (collecting it precisely), and any light source placed at the focus of a headlight's parabolic reflector sends all light straight out as a parallel beam.
Meaning 6: The Primary Site of a Disease (Medicine)

In medical and clinical language, the focus of a disease or infection is the main location in the body where it is concentrated or where it began.

"The focus of the infection was identified in the lower left lung."
"The tumour represented a single focus of disease."
Meaning 7: Purpose and Direction in Life (Informal)

In casual, everyday speech, focus can refer to a sense of clear direction or purpose — knowing what you want and working toward it without being lost or scattered.

"She really needs some focus in her life."
"The program gave the students a sense of focus and ambition."

This is a natural extension of meaning 1 (the mental state of concentration), stretched to describe a person's overall orientation in life rather than attention in a single moment.
The Thread Running Through All Meanings

Every meaning of focus shares the same underlying idea: a single, definite, central point around which everything else is organized. Whether it's the underground point where an earthquake starts, the optical point where light converges, the special point defining a geometric shape, the site of a medical problem, or the thing your mind is locked onto — it is always the one central point that matters most, that everything else is arranged in relation to.
Common Phrases and Expressions

• In focus — sharp, clear, properly centred. Used literally (images) and metaphorically (ideas, plans).
  • Out of focus — blurry, unclear, not properly centred.
  • Come into focus — to gradually become clear. "After months of uncertainty, his plan finally came into focus."
  • Bring into focus — to make something clear or visible. "The report brought the real costs into focus."
  • The focus of — the main subject or centre of something. "The focus of the inquiry was the financial records."
  • Shift the focus — to change what is being attended to. "She shifted the focus of the conversation to something lighter."
  • Lose focus — to become distracted, to stop concentrating.
  • Regain/maintain focus — to bring concentration back or keep it steady.
  • Sharp focus — extremely clear and precise attention or image. "The issue was thrown into sharp focus by the crisis."
  • Central/main/primary focus — the most important subject of attention.
The Plural Forms

The standard English plural is focuses, used in everyday contexts.

"The report covers several focuses: health, education, and housing."

In scientific and technical writing — particularly in geometry, optics, and medicine — the Latin plural foci (say it as two syllables: FOH-sye) is widely used and preferred.

"An ellipse has two foci."
"Multiple foci of infection were found."

Both forms are correct; the choice is mostly about register (everyday English vs. scientific/technical writing).
